ideas.title: Cairn Climbers
ideas.concept: A push-your-luck dexterity game where players draw route tiles that dictate risky additions to a shared central stone cairn, blindly drawing weighted 'stones' from a bag and stacking them one-handed to bank points before it topples. Every turn is a real physical bet: bank now, or draw one more route tile and reach higher into the pile knowing a single wobble erases your gains for the round.
ideas.differentiation: Combines blind-draw weight uncertainty (you don't know a stone's size class until it's in your hand) with route-tile scoring constraints on a shared communal stack, rather than a personal tower. Searched 'dexterity stacking board game mountain climbing rocks push your luck' and 'stacking dexterity games' — found Junk Art (personal stacking, all pieces visible/chosen) and Dicey Peaks/High Risk (dice-based mountain climbing with no physical stacking at all); no shipped product combines blind-weight-class stone draws with a shared cairn and route-tile scoring constraints.
ideas.rules: 2-5 players. Setup: place the Base Plate in the table center; fill the Scree Bowl with all 60 stone pieces (mixed pebbles/stones/boulders); shuffle the 40 Route Tiles face-down in a stack; each player takes a Score Track marker set to 0. On your turn: reveal the top Route Tile (it states a requirement, e.g. 'draw 2 stones, at least 1 must be a boulder' and a point value). Choose to Attempt or Pass. If you Attempt: reach into the Scree Bowl without looking and draw stones one at a time, placing each immediately onto the cairn using only one hand, touching only already-placed pieces, until you've met the tile's requirement. If the cairn (or any piece being placed) falls off the Base Plate at any point, your attempt fails: score 0 for the tile, return all fallen pieces to the bowl, turn passes. If you succeed, you may Bank the tile's points immediately, or Push Further by revealing another Route Tile and attempting again (points only score if you eventually Bank; failing after pushing forfeits everything drawn that turn). Play passes clockwise after each turn resolves. The game ends when the Route Tile stack is exhausted or the Scree Bowl is emptied twice; the player with the highest banked score wins, ties broken by fewest failed attempts.
ideas.components: 1x Base Plate (PLA, 150mm diameter textured disc marking the legal cairn footprint); 60x Stone pieces in 3 weight/size classes (20 pebbles ~15mm, 20 stones ~25mm, 20 boulders ~35mm, irregular rock-shaped PLA with flattened printed contact facets for stackability, varied infill density per class for realistic heft); 1x Scree Bowl (PLA, 180mm diameter opaque bowl); 40x Route Tiles (PLA engraved discs, 35mm diameter x3mm, requirement/points debossed and painted); 5x Score Track boards (PLA, 100x40mm strip with a sliding peg marker); 5x Score peg markers (PLA, 8mm); 1x storage box (PLA, two-piece lidded box, 220x220x90mm, with a foam-free tray insert dividing stone weight classes).
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity/stacking games are a well-established BGG category (Stacking Dexterity Games list on BGG spans 50+ titles; Junk Art and Rhino Hero are perennial top-100-selling family dexterity games per multiple retailer bestseller trackers). Push-your-luck as a mechanic ranks among BGG's most-used tags across 1,000+ games. Target audience: family game night and party groups, ages 8+, players who enjoy tactile risk (Jenga/Junk Art buyers).
ideas.fun_case: Each turn's core tension is a real physical bet under time pressure — bank a known small score or risk everything for a bigger one, mirroring the proven appeal of Can't Stop and Incan Gold's push-your-luck loop but made tactile and social since everyone watches the hands shake. Blind stone draws (unknown weight until it's in your hand) add a genuine skill/luck blend that Junk Art (fully visible pieces) doesn't have. 15-25 minute playtime and one-sentence rules fit family/party audiences the same way Junk Art and Rhino Hero do.
ideas.producibility_notes: 20 distinct stone geometries (organic rock shapes) is the biggest part-count item but all print as single-piece FDM objects with flat printable base facets — no supports needed if oriented correctly, no assembly. Route tiles and score tracks are flat engraved/debossed discs, standard FDM text legibility at 3mm depth. No hinges, no snap-fits, no hardware inserts anywhere in the BOM — this is the lowest-joint-risk idea in the set. Riskiest tolerance: stone base facets must be flat enough (within ~0.3mm) to actually balance when stacked, which is a slicer/orientation concern, not a novel unvalidated mechanism — physical stacking behavior itself is a long-validated genre (Junk Art, Rhino Hero, Bausack all ship successfully on the same physics).

In front, a round stone-grey 3D-printed base plate holds a precarious tower of irregular rock-shaped pieces in three sizes (small tan pebbles, medium grey stones, large brown boulders) stacked in a wobbly cairn. ideas.title: Whistleblower
ideas.concept: A hidden-role deduction game for 5-8 players where secret ballots are cast by inserting colored pegs into a two-layer Suspicion Board, then revealed all at once by rotating an opaque cover ring — no cards, no talking sheets, just a satisfying physical unveiling of who the table pointed at. Citizens must unmask the Informants before the Informants quietly out-number them.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'social deduction board game rotating suspicion dial physical tracker instead of cards' and 'suspicion board game' twice with different phrasing — found only Suspicion (Wonder Forge, card+dice based) and generic dial/counter accessories on Etsy, none of which use a rotating dual-layer reveal mechanism for simultaneous secret voting. The specific mechanism (fixed hole-layer + rotating opaque flap-layer that aligns on rotation to reveal all votes at once) is not found as an existing shipped social deduction product.
ideas.rules: 5-8 players. Setup: each player secretly draws an ID Chip (blank side up) — in a 5-6 player game there are 2 Informant chips, in 7-8 player games there are 3, rest are Citizens; keep your chip hidden. Place the two-layer Suspicion Board in the center (bottom layer has one numbered hole per player; top layer is an opaque ring with hinged flap-covered slots, currently closed/offset so no holes are visible). Each round has two phases. Discussion (open timer, 3 minutes): players talk freely, accuse, defend. Suspicion (simultaneous, hidden): each player, shielded by their personal Privacy Screen, inserts one colored peg into the hole numbered for whoever they suspect most. Once everyone has voted, any player rotates the top ring 90 degrees clockwise until it clicks into the Reveal position, aligning the flap slots over the holes and popping all pegs into view at once. The player with the most pegs is publicly Accused; their ID Chip flips face-up. If they were an Informant, Citizens place a token on the Truth Track (Citizens win outright at 2 tokens for 5-6p games, 3 for 7-8p). If they were a Citizen, remove them from the game (they no longer vote or discuss) and Informants gain a bonus peg (2 votes) next round. Reset the board and repeat. Informants win if, at any point, the number of remaining unrevealed Informants equals or exceeds the number of remaining unrevealed Citizens.
ideas.components: 1x Suspicion Board bottom layer (PLA, 200mm diameter disc, 8 numbered through-holes); 1x Suspicion Board top ring (PLA, 200mm diameter rotating ring with hinged flap-slots, center pivot peg + retaining cap, 4-position rotational detents); 8x ID Chips (PLA, 30mm hexagonal chips, one face blank, other face engraved 'CITIZEN' or 'INFORMANT', double-sided printed then painted); 8x Privacy Screens (PLA, folded L-shaped stand-up shields, 100x80mm); 20x Voting Pegs in 8 player colors (PLA, 10mm cylindrical pegs, 2-3 per player); 1x Truth Track board (PLA, 150x40mm strip with slide markers for both factions); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 230x230x60mm with a molded peg/chip tray).
ideas.demand_case: Social deduction is one of BGG's largest active categories (900+ games tagged, Werewolf/Mafia-style formats have sustained party-game bestseller status for 20+ years; Secret Hitler and The Resistance both rank in BGG's top 200 overall). Target audience: party/social groups of 5-8, ages 12+, the existing buyer base for Werewolf, Secret Hitler, and Avalon looking for a fresh physical gimmick rather than another card deck.
ideas.fun_case: The core weekly tension of every social-deduction game — reading the table, deciding who to protect or expose — is preserved, but the simultaneous physical reveal (all pegs popping into view at once via the rotating ring) replaces slow card-flip reveals with a single shared dramatic beat that a whole table watches together, which is the same reason Secret Hitler's simultaneous policy reveal is consistently cited as its most memorable moment. 30-45 minute playtime and simple peg-voting rules match the established party audience for Werewolf-style games.
ideas.producibility_notes: 9 unique printed parts total; the reveal mechanism is a single rotating disc on a center pivot peg with printed detent notches — a well-validated FDM joint type (same family as a lazy-susan bearing-free pivot), not a novel unvalidated mechanism, since its only job is hole alignment, not weight-bearing or balance. Smallest feature is the engraved chip text at ~1.5mm stroke width, within standard FDM legibility at 0.2mm layer height. Riskiest tolerance is the ring-to-base pivot clearance (needs ~0.2-0.3mm play to rotate smoothly without wobble that misaligns holes) — a known, testable slicer tolerance, not a physics-dependent unknown.

Beside it, open and in play: a round two-layer 3D-printed suspicion board in dark grey with a lighter rotating outer ring showing small hinged flaps, several colored pegs (red, blue, yellow, green) visible in numbered holes. Around the board, small hexagonal ID chips face-down, a few folding privacy screens standing upright, and a slim wooden-toned truth-track strip with sliding markers. Cinematic noir lighting, deep shadows, red and grey accent palette.

ideas.title: Orbital Blockade
ideas.concept: The 2,000-year-old strategy classic Nine Men's Morris, restyled as a near-future satellite war: players place and slide satellite tokens along printed orbital lattice lines, forming three-in-a-row 'supply lines' to disable an opponent's satellites, aiming to reduce them to two pieces or block all their legal moves.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Nine Men's Morris (public domain, unchanged ruleset — placement phase, movement phase, mills capture enemy pieces). Styling concept: the flat cross-hatch board is restyled as a radial orbital lattice (concentric ring 'orbits' connected by spoke 'transfer lanes') and pieces restyled as two-tone satellite tokens with solar-panel geometry, mills renamed 'supply lines.' Searched 'nine men's morris space station theme reskin board game' and 'nine men's morris board game etsy' — found only traditional wood/leather/marble aesthetic versions (medieval, nautical, rustic); no space/orbital-themed version located as an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 2 players, 9 pieces each (Satellites). Setup: empty orbital board (3 concentric ring 'orbits' connected by transfer-lane spokes at 8 intersection points per ring, 24 nodes total, standard Nine Men's Morris topology). Phase 1 - Deployment: players alternate placing one Satellite on any empty node until both have placed all 9. Whenever a player completes three of their own Satellites in a straight line along an orbit or spoke (a 'Supply Line'), they immediately remove one opponent Satellite of their choice (not from an opponent's own completed Supply Line unless no other option exists). Phase 2 - Maneuver: once all pieces are placed, players alternate sliding one of their Satellites to an adjacent empty node along a printed connection line (no jumps); forming a new Supply Line (including by re-breaking and reforming one) again removes an opponent piece under the same rule. A player who has been reduced to exactly 2 Satellites, or who has no legal moves on their turn, loses immediately.
ideas.components: 1x Orbital board (PLA, 250mm diameter flat disc, printed/painted radial lattice of 3 rings + 8 spokes, 24 recessed node dimples); 18x Satellite tokens (PLA, 9 per player in two colors, 20mm discs with printed solar-panel wing detail, flat bottom peg to seat in node dimples); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 270x270x30mm, board doubles as box lid inset).
ideas.demand_case: Nine Men's Morris is one of the most continuously played abstract strategy games in history, with active tournament scenes and dedicated retail listings across Etsy, Amazon, and specialty game shops; BGG lists it with 1,000+ ratings despite predating modern publishing. Target audience: abstract-strategy fans and casual two-player households looking for a portable, quick (10-20 min) game with a fresh sci-fi look — the same buyers who purchase themed chess/checkers sets.
ideas.fun_case: The decision each turn — where to place or slide to build a three-in-a-row while blocking the opponent's — is the same tight, well-proven tension that has kept Nine Men's Morris played for two millennia; the reskin changes nothing about that math, only the visual hook, so fun is inherited wholesale from a mechanically-solved classic (like themed chess sets validate for chess). 10-20 minute playtime suits quick two-player sessions and travel/gift purchases.
ideas.producibility_notes: Only 2 unique part types (board, token), no assembly, no hinges or inserts. Node dimples are simple 3-4mm deep recesses, well within FDM tolerance; token seating pegs are a loose peg-in-dimple fit (no press-fit precision required since pieces aren't meant to lock in place — they must slide freely). Lowest-risk producibility item in the set alongside Meteor Field.
ideas.prompt: Product photo on a deep-space navy backdrop with subtle star specks: a sleek black game box titled 'ORBITAL BLOCKADE' in metallic silver lettering with a stylized ringed-planet icon. In front, a circular 3D-printed game board in matte dark grey showing a glowing radial lattice of orbit rings and transfer-lane spokes, dotted with small satellite tokens — one set in cyan-blue with tiny solar-panel wings, the other in molten-orange — positioned mid-game along the lattice. Cool blue rim lighting, sci-fi product photography style, navy and metallic-silver palette.

ideas.title: Riverworks
ideas.concept: A pick-up-and-deliver trading game on a modular canal network where boats can only pass through lock gates if their cargo weight is at or below that gate's current physical water level — a printed slider peg you or your rivals must spend actions to raise or lower. Every delivery run is a puzzle of routing around locks you don't control and timing when to spend an action opening one for everyone.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'canal lock water level board game pipe connection movable peg gauge' and 'canal lock river board game physical water level gauge component' — results returned only real-world canal infrastructure signage and digital pipe-puzzle apps, no shipped tabletop game using a physical sliding-peg lock-level gauge as a pass/fail gate mechanic for a pickup-and-deliver network. Pick-up-and-deliver itself is a well-documented BGG mechanic (Empire Builder, Age of Steam) but none use a shared physical lock-level component that any player can alter.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: assemble the modular hex Canal Tiles into a river network connecting 6 Village hexes (commodity sources) and 6 Market hexes (delivery destinations); place a Lock Gate token (with a 3-position sliding peg, starting at Mid) at each of the 5 marked chokepoints between tile sections; each player takes a Boat pawn and 3 Cargo tokens of their color, starting at a random Village. Shuffle the Contract Tiles (each shows a source commodity, a destination Market, and a point value) into a face-up row of 4. On your turn, take up to 3 actions from: Move (slide your Boat one hex along a connected canal path — you may only cross a Lock Gate hex if your currently-loaded Cargo's printed weight number is less than or equal to the gate's current peg position); Load (pick up a Cargo token matching your current Village's commodity, max 2 carried at once); Adjust Lock (spend 1 action and 1 Lock Key resource token to slide any one Lock Gate's peg up or down one notch — this benefits all players, not just you); Deliver (if at a matching Market with the required Cargo, claim a face-up Contract Tile, score its points, discard the Cargo, refill the Contract row). Game ends when the Contract deck is exhausted; highest total points wins.
ideas.components: 18x Canal Tiles (PLA, 60mm hex tiles with printed canal-path grooves, edge-matching connectors); 6x Village hex overlays and 6x Market hex overlays (PLA, 60mm hex toppers, distinct commodity/market icon each); 5x Lock Gate tokens (PLA, 40x25mm two-part assembly: a slotted frame + a sliding peg with 3 printed detent notches Low/Mid/High); 4x Boat pawns (PLA, 25mm, one per player color); 24x Cargo tokens (PLA, 15mm cubes in 6 commodity colors, each debossed with a weight number 1-3); 20x Contract Tiles (PLA, 40mm engraved discs showing source/destination/points); 16x Lock Key tokens (PLA, 12mm brass-look chips); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 250x250x70mm with tile-nesting tray).
ideas.demand_case: Pick-up-and-deliver is a long-established, actively-tracked BGG mechanic with dozens of well-rated titles (Empire Builder franchise, Firefly, Mombasa) and a dedicated fan geeklist with 100+ community entries. Modular hex tile-laying (Catan-style) is independently one of the best-selling board game formats of the last two decades. Target audience: mid-weight euro-strategy gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy route optimization and light player interaction without direct combat.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn — spend your limited actions moving cargo, or spend one improving a shared lock that also helps your rivals — creates the same tense cooperative/competitive tension that makes Age of Steam's shared track auctions and Container's shared shipping lanes engaging, but resolved through a tactile physical gate you can see and feel change state rather than an abstract track. 45-75 minute playtime and moderate rules complexity (roughly Ticket to Ride-plus) fit the stated mid-weight euro audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 24 unique part types is the highest part-count item in this set, but complexity is manageable: hex tiles and overlays are flat prints with edge-matching grooves (no tight tolerance needed, grooves are visual/routing guides not physical connectors). The one genuinely mechanical part is the Lock Gate slider — a peg in a slotted frame with 3 printed detent bumps, a known, validated FDM slider-with-detents joint (same family as a printed drawer latch), not a novel or physics-dependent mechanism; recommend 0.3-0.4mm clearance between peg and slot walls for smooth-but-retained sliding. No hardware inserts required anywhere.

On the table, an assembled hexagonal canal network of blue-grooved tiles winding between small village and market hex toppers, dotted with tiny colorful cargo cubes and four painted boat pawns in red, blue, yellow, and green. ideas.title: Ember Court
ideas.concept: A trick-taking game played with double-sided engraved tiles where the front (suit and rank) is all you ever see during play, but the back carries a hidden ember glyph you only discover when you flip your entire pile of won tricks at round's end. You're not just fighting to win tricks for points — you're fighting blind for a stack of mystery bonuses you won't understand until the round is over.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: standard follow-suit trick-taking (the family that includes Hearts, Skull King, and dozens of domino-based trick games). Specific rule change: tiles are double-sided with a hidden reverse glyph that is never read during play and only revealed simultaneously by all players at end-of-round when they flip their captured-trick stacks, converting trick-winning from a purely score-now decision into a blind bet on unknown future bonuses/penalties. Searched 'trick taking card game double-sided cards hidden bonus revealed end of round scoring' and 'domino trick taking game tile flip orientation changes trump suit' — found Double Side Play (reads a different printed side mid-round for bidding, not a hidden-until-round-end reveal) and Pavlova (domino trick-taking with in-play orientation choice affecting trump strength). Neither uses a permanently-hidden reverse face revealed only at round-end for a separate bonus-scoring layer; this specific combination was not found as an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players. Deck: 45 tiles, 5 suits (Ember colors) ranked 1-9, each tile's reverse face bears one of 4 hidden Glyphs (Flame, Frost, Wind, Ash) distributed randomly and fixed at manufacture (glyphs are not visible during setup or play — tiles are placed reverse-down in the draw pool and dealt face-down, only turned face-up to be played). Deal all tiles evenly (adjust hand size for player count, discard remainder face-down unseen). Standard trick-taking: leader plays any tile face-up; other players must follow the led suit if able, otherwise may play any tile; highest rank of the led suit wins the trick unless a designated Trump suit (rotates each round) is played, in which case highest Trump wins. The trick winner takes all played tiles and stacks them face-up (visible rank/suit) but does not look at the backs, adding them to their personal Hearth Stack. Play continues until hands are empty. End of round: each player simultaneously flips their entire Hearth Stack to reveal all glyphs at once. Score: 1 point per tile won (rank irrelevant to base score) + bonus for glyph sets (3+ matching glyphs = +5, 4 matching = +10) − 1 point per Ash glyph collected. Play 3 rounds, reshuffling and redealing each round; highest total score wins.
ideas.components: 45x Ember Tiles (PLA, 40x60mm rectangular tiles, front face engraved with suit icon + rank number in 5 colors, back face engraved with one of 4 glyph icons, both faces painted); 5x Trump Indicator tokens (PLA, 20mm discs, one per suit, used to mark the round's trump); 4x Player Hearth Stack trays (PLA, 70x100mm shallow tray to keep each player's won-tricks pile aligned for the simultaneous flip); 1x Score Track board (PLA, 300x50mm strip with 4 sliding peg markers); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 200x150x60mm with a tile-slot insert tray).
ideas.demand_case: Trick-taking is one of BGG's most active mechanic categories (2,000+ games tagged); modern trick-taking titles like Skull King and The Crew have each sold hundreds of thousands of copies and maintain BGG ratings above 7.5 with tens of thousands of ratings. Target audience: card-game-mechanic fans, ages 10+, family/game-night groups who already own Hearts/Skull King-style games and want a fresh hook.
ideas.fun_case: The central decision each trick — fight to win it or dump a low tile to avoid it — is trick-taking's proven core tension (validated by decades of Hearts and modern hits like The Crew), but the hidden-glyph twist adds a genuine second layer: winning tricks is no longer straightforwardly good, since you're blindly accumulating unknown bonuses or penalties, creating the same 'was that actually good for me?' suspense that makes Hearts' Queen of Spades meaningful, generalized across every trick rather than one card. 20-30 minute rounds and simple follow-suit rules fit the stated family/game-night audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 45 unique double-sided tiles is a moderate part-count but each is a single flat print requiring two-pass engraving (front and back), a standard FDM/CNC-adjacent workflow, no assembly or joints at all. Smallest feature is the glyph icon at approximately 8mm diameter with 1mm line detail, within safe FDM resolution at 0.2mm nozzle. No hinges, pivots, or inserts anywhere in the BOM — second-lowest joint risk in this set after Cairn Climbers/Orbital Blockade.

Fanned across the cloth, rectangular engraved tiles in five jewel-tone colors (ruby, sapphire, amber, emerald, violet) showing suit icons and numbers face-up, with a few tiles flipped to show mysterious flame, frost, wind, and ash glyphs on their backs. Small shallow wooden-toned trays hold neat stacks of won tiles, and a slim scoring strip with colored pegs sits to the side. Warm candlelit glow, deep red and gold palette, dramatic side lighting.

ideas.title: Foundry Row
ideas.concept: A worker placement game where every action slot along a shared Forge Line shifts value each round via a rotating index wheel, so the action you placed a worker on this round quietly becomes a different, often better or worse, action by the time you retrieve it. Reading the wheel and timing your placements against a slot's drift is the whole game.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: worker placement with a time-delay retrieval element (the family Tzolk'in: The Mayan Calendar popularized, where workers left longer on rotating gears yield stronger actions). Specific rule change: instead of the gears themselves physically carrying workers in a circle, workers sit in fixed numbered slots on a static Forge Line board, and a separate rotating Index Wheel (read via an aligned window, not a mechanism that moves the workers) determines which printed action each slot currently maps to, changing every round — a lookup-table twist rather than a worker-carrying gear. Searched 'interlocking gear tiles board game worker placement mechanism' (found Tzolk'in, which physically rotates workers on gears) and 'conveyor belt moving track worker placement board game workers pushed forward each round' (found Steam Works, whose belt cycles available resource tiles, not placed workers). Neither moves workers via a static-slot/rotating-lookup-wheel combination; this specific mechanism is not found as an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the Forge Line board (10 numbered action slots in a row) and the Index Wheel (a rotating disc with a single reveal window, marked 0-9, aligned above the Forge Line) at 0. Each player takes 3 Worker pawns and starts with 5 Ore tokens. Round structure: (1) Placement — in turn order, each player places 1 unplaced Worker on any empty Forge Line slot; (2) Resolution — starting from slot 0 and moving up, each occupied slot's current action is determined by reading the Action Reference card at position (slot number + Index Wheel value) mod 10, and that action resolves immediately for the worker's owner (actions include: gain 2 Ore, gain 1 Blueprint tile, trade 3 Ore for 1 Artifact tile, or — if the computed position lands on the printed Furnace action — the worker is automatically returned to its owner with a bonus Artifact tile, ending that worker's turn early); (3) Advance — rotate the Index Wheel forward by 2 positions; (4) any Workers still on the Forge Line remain there into the next round (their action will differ next round since the Wheel has moved) unless their owner spends an action to manually recall them (recalling forfeits that round's action but returns the worker to hand). Game ends after 8 rounds; score 1 point per Ore, 2 per Blueprint, 4 per Artifact; highest score wins.
ideas.components: 1x Forge Line board (PLA, 400x60mm strip with 10 numbered recessed worker slots); 1x Index Wheel assembly (PLA, 120mm rotating disc on a center pivot peg with printed reveal window frame, 10-position detents); Action reference printed directly as a fixed engraved ring around the Forge Line board (no separate card component); 12x Worker pawns (PLA, 22mm, 3 per player in 4 colors); 60x Ore tokens (PLA, 10mm hex chips, bronze-painted); 20x Blueprint tiles (PLA, 25mm square chips); 12x Artifact tiles (PLA, 30mm engraved discs); 4x Player reference boards (PLA, 100x70mm); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 260x180x60mm with tray insert).
ideas.demand_case: Worker placement is BGG's largest strategy-mechanic category by game count (3,500+ tagged titles); Tzolk'in alone holds a BGG rank in the top 150 overall with 25,000+ ratings, demonstrating strong sustained demand for rotating-mechanism worker placement specifically. Target audience: mid-to-heavy euro strategy gamers, ages 12+, who own or want Tzolk'in-adjacent games.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each round — place a worker on a slot betting on what it'll become once the wheel turns, versus recalling a worker early to lock in a known result — is a direct, validated descendant of Tzolk'in's 'place now for a worse immediate action or a better delayed one' tension, which is widely cited as that game's standout hook. 60-90 minute playtime and moderate-heavy complexity match the stated euro-gamer audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 9 unique part types; the one mechanical component is the Index Wheel, a rotating disc on a center pivot peg with a fixed window frame — identical validated joint family to the reveal mechanisms in Whistleblower and Spice Route Caravan (reusing a proven pivot-disc design across the line reduces risk further, since the joint type has been independently reasoned through three times). No hardware inserts required; recommend 0.25-0.3mm pivot clearance for smooth rotation without wobble. No components require physical prototyping to validate fairness — the Furnace/action outcomes are deterministic lookups, not physics-dependent.

In front, a long horizontal 3D-printed action strip with ten numbered worker slots holding small pawns in four colors (red, blue, yellow, green), and beside it a circular rotating index wheel with a small reveal window showing a number. Warm forge-glow lighting, industrial orange-and-steel palette, dramatic overhead product shot.

ideas.title: Spice Route Caravan
ideas.concept: A hex-tile caravan trading game where a central rotating Bazaar Wheel determines which commodity is currently most valuable, and every sale you make rotates it forward — so the market you're racing toward reshuffles itself with every trade made by anyone at the table, including your rivals. You're never just planning a route; you're planning a route against a price you know is about to move.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: pick-up-and-deliver trading with a market/price element (the family that includes Merchant of Venus and various commodity-trading designs, some going back to 1970s-era patented 'price wheel' trading-game apparatuses). Specific rule change: the price wheel is not a private per-player pricing tool but a single shared disc that any player's sale action rotates, so pricing dynamically shifts for everyone based on cumulative trade activity, combined with a modular hex-tile caravan route network (a structural pairing not found in the older price-wheel patents, which used fixed circular maps, not player-built modular route tiles). Searched 'pickup and deliver trading board game rotating commodity price dial wheel component' and 'rotating price wheel board game dynamic pricing trading mechanic' — found only a 1970s-era commodity board game patent (fixed map, not modular tiles, not a shipped consumer product) and BGG forum discussion of dynamic pricing generally with no specific matching shipped title; narrowing the claim to the shared-wheel-plus-modular-hex-network combination specifically, since the wheel mechanism alone has older, non-shipped prior art.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: assemble Desert Hex tiles into a route network connecting 6 City hexes, each producing one of 6 commodities; place the Bazaar Wheel (a rotating disc with all 6 commodities around its rim) in the center, pointer fixed at commodity position 1 (highest price). Each player starts with a Caravan pawn at a random City and 10 gold. On your turn, take up to 3 actions from: Move (advance your Caravan 1 hex along the network); Buy (at your current City, purchase 1-3 units of that City's commodity at base cost 2 gold each, load onto your Caravan, max capacity 4 units); Sell (at any City, sell any commodity for gold equal to its current price as read off the Bazaar Wheel's rim at the pointer, then rotate the Wheel one detent (60 degrees) clockwise — this changes which commodity now sits at the highest-price pointer position for all players' future sales); Fulfill Contract (if carrying the exact commodities a face-up Contract Tile requires, turn it in for bonus gold and draw a new one). Game ends after any player reaches 40 gold or 15 rounds elapse; highest gold total wins.
ideas.components: 24x Desert Hex tiles (PLA, 55mm hex, printed route/dune texture, edge-matching path notches); 6x City hex overlays (PLA, 55mm hex toppers, unique commodity icon each); 1x Bazaar Wheel assembly (PLA, 150mm rotating disc with 6 commodity icons around the rim on a center pivot peg, fixed pointer arm, 6-position detents); 4x Caravan pawns (PLA, 25mm camel-shaped, one per player color); 36x Commodity tokens (PLA, 12mm hex chips in 6 colors); 16x Contract Tiles (PLA, 35mm engraved discs); 4x Gold trackers (PLA, 100x30mm slider strips with peg markers); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 250x250x70mm with hex tray insert).
ideas.demand_case: Pick-up-and-deliver and commodity-trading mechanics are both long-tracked, actively-played BGG categories (Pick-up and Deliver mechanic page lists 400+ titles; trading-game fans sustain multi-decade franchises like Merchant of Venus and Catan's trade mechanic). Target audience: mid-weight euro/trading-game players, ages 10+, who enjoy Catan-adjacent hex-network games with more economic depth.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension each turn — sell now at a good price knowing you'll shift the market against yourself, or hold out and risk a rival selling first and moving the wheel unfavorably — mirrors the proven appeal of shared-resource-scarcity tension in Catan (where trading a resource changes its relative value to the table) but made visible and mechanical via a single shared dial everyone watches. 45-60 minute playtime and moderate complexity fit the stated mid-weight trading-game audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: The Bazaar Wheel reuses the same validated pivot-disc-with-detents joint family as Whistleblower's reveal ring and Foundry Row's Index Wheel (a third independent application of the same low-risk mechanism type). Hex tiles and overlays are flat prints with visual-only edge notches, no physical connector tolerance required. No hardware inserts anywhere. Highest part-count item after Riverworks, but part complexity is uniformly low (flat tiles, one pivot disc, flat chips).

On the table, an assembled network of sandy hexagonal tiles with dune-groove texture connecting small city hex toppers marked with commodity icons (spice, silk, salt, gem, dye, incense). At the center, a circular rotating wheel shows six commodity icons around its rim with a fixed brass-look pointer. Small camel-shaped caravan pawns in four colors sit along the route, surrounded by colorful hexagonal commodity chips and engraved contract discs. ideas.title: Meteor Field
ideas.concept: The classic 33-hole peg solitaire puzzle, restyled as clearing a field of asteroid debris toward a central singularity, playable solo as a puzzle or head-to-head in a race variant where two identical boards go simultaneously and the first to whittle their debris down to a single remaining piece wins.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: English peg solitaire (public domain, unchanged jump-and-capture rules on the standard 33-hole cross board). Styling concept: pegs restyled as glow-cast asteroid debris chunks, the board restyled as a radiating meteor field with a dark 'singularity' center hole, plus an included printed 2-board Race Variant frame for competitive head-to-head play (a documented but less common peg-solitaire format). Searched 'peg solitaire space meteor theme reskin board game' — found only generic customizable-theme references and standard wood/classic versions (Kubiya Games, Cracker Barrel-style); no space/asteroid/meteor-themed shipped version located.
ideas.rules: Solo mode (1 player): standard English peg solitaire — 33 holes in a cross shape, all filled with pegs except the center hole. A peg may jump over an adjacent peg into an empty hole in a straight line (horizontal or vertical, no diagonals), removing the jumped peg. Continue jumping (each jump is a separate move) until no more jumps are possible. Goal: end with as few pegs remaining as possible, ideally 1, ideally in the center hole. Race variant (2 players): each player gets an identical board and peg set, both starting from the same standard setup, playing simultaneously and independently (no shared board, no direct interaction) — first player to reach exactly 1 remaining peg calls 'Singularity!' and wins; if both get stuck with more than 1 peg remaining, whoever has fewer pegs left wins.
ideas.components: 2x Meteor Field boards (PLA, 200mm diameter dark-textured disc with 33 recessed peg holes radiating from a printed 'singularity' center); 66x Debris pegs (PLA, 33 per board, 12mm irregular asteroid-chunk-shaped pegs with a cylindrical base pin sized to seat in the board holes); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 220x220x40mm with peg-tray insert, doubles as a single-board case if only solo play is desired).
ideas.demand_case: Peg solitaire is one of the most widely recognized and continuously sold puzzle games in the world (the Cracker Barrel restaurant chain's tabletop version alone is a widely-cited pop-culture touchstone in the US, and multiple retailers list dozens of peg solitaire SKUs). Target audience: puzzle-game buyers and casual gift purchasers, ages 6+, including the solo-puzzle audience and, via the race variant, casual head-to-head players.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each move — which jump sequence clears the board most efficiently, since an early bad jump can strand pegs permanently — is a well-proven, decades-validated single-player logic puzzle loop (the reason peg solitaire remains a bestselling puzzle format), and the added race variant gives it a genuine social/competitive angle that most shipped peg solitaire sets don't offer. 5-15 minute playtime per game supports quick solo sessions or repeated head-to-head rounds.
ideas.producibility_notes: Only 2 unique part types (board, peg), no assembly, no joints beyond a simple peg-in-hole friction fit (loosest tolerance category, ~0.3-0.5mm clearance, extremely well-validated across countless printed peg games). Lowest-risk producibility item in the entire set alongside Orbital Blockade and Cairn Climbers.
ideas.prompt: Product photo on a deep black starfield backdrop with faint nebula wisps: a sleek dark purple game box titled 'METEOR FIELD' in glowing cyan lettering with a small singularity icon. In front, a dark circular 3D-printed board with a radiating cross pattern of recessed holes, filled with small glow-toned asteroid-chunk pegs in muted grey and rust-orange, one hole empty at the exact center showing a tiny glowing singularity marker. A second identical board sits nearby for the race variant. Cool cyan-purple rim lighting, cosmic minimalist palette, dramatic top-down product shot.

ideas.title: Loom & Ledger
ideas.concept: A blind-bidding trade game where you buy patterned silk tiles at auction using a strictly limited personal coin supply (no bank makes change, so overbidding can leave you unable to bid precisely again), then immediately weave won tiles into your personal tapestry board where matching-color adjacency multiplies their value. Every bid is a double gamble: can you afford it now, and will it actually score once it's placed?
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: blind simultaneous-bid auction for goods, the family popularized by For Sale (Stefan Dorra), where players commit money face-down and the highest secret bid wins each lot. Specific rule change: bidding uses a fixed, non-replenishing personal supply of discrete coin denominations (2x each of value 1/3/5/10, no bank change-making of any kind, so spending a 10-coin on a 4-value bid wastes 6 permanently), and won tiles must be placed immediately onto a personal grid board where color-adjacency multiplies their end-game value, layering a placement-puzzle scoring system onto the blind-bid auction. Searched 'board game nested coin tokens make change bidding mechanic physical' and 'secret bidding mechanics board game' — found general blind-bidding mechanic pages and For Sale itself (which uses paper money with full change-making by the bank) plus dexterity-bidding variants (Hibachi); no shipped blind-bidding game found that removes bank change-making via fixed discrete coin counts combined with a placement-adjacency scoring board.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: each player takes a personal Loom Board (5x5 grid) and a coin set of 2x value-1, 2x value-3, 2x value-5, 1x value-10 coins (21 total value). Shuffle the 40 Silk Tiles (each shows a color and a base value 1-6) and reveal 1 per active player each round in a market row. Bidding (simultaneous, blind): each player selects any combination of their own coins totaling their intended bid and places them face-down in front of them (no bank, no change — whatever coins you commit are spent regardless of whether they exceed the tile's value). All bids reveal simultaneously; for each tile in the market row (highest value tile first), the highest bidder takes that tile and permanently discards their committed coins to the box (not to a bank — coins are gone from the game for that player); ties are broken in favor of whoever has fewer coins remaining. Each won tile must be placed immediately onto an empty cell of your Loom Board, orthogonally adjacent to at least one previously placed tile if any exist. End of game (after all 40 tiles are distributed or any player cannot place a won tile): score each tile's base value, doubled for each orthogonally-adjacent tile sharing its exact color (e.g., a value-4 tile touching two same-color tiles scores 4x3=12); highest total wins.
ideas.components: 4x Loom Boards (PLA, 5x5 grid, 150x150mm, recessed square cells sized for tiles); 40x Silk Tiles (PLA, 28mm square chips in 6 colors, engraved with base value); 28x Coin tokens (PLA, 4 denominations across 4 player sets: 8x value-1 at 15mm, 8x value-3 at 18mm, 8x value-5 at 22mm, 4x value-10 at 26mm, each debossed with its value); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 220x220x60mm with a coin-tray insert sorted by denomination).
ideas.demand_case: Blind/simultaneous bidding is a well-established BGG mechanic (500+ tagged titles); For Sale itself has sustained 20,000+ BGG ratings and remains in active reprint decades after release, demonstrating durable demand for exactly this bidding format. Target audience: family/light-strategy gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy For Sale, Ra, or other bidding-driven titles and want an added spatial-puzzle layer.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each round — commit exact-value coins you can't get back, knowing overbidding cripples your future precision — is a sharper, more consequential version of For Sale's proven simultaneous-bid tension (validated by two decades of continuous sales), and the adjacency-scoring placement layer adds the same kind of 'where does this actually go' puzzle tension that makes tile-laying games like Kingdomino engaging, combined rather than left separate. 30-45 minute playtime and light-medium complexity fit the stated family/light-strategy audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 unique part types (board, tile, coin-in-4-sizes) with no assembly and no joints — coins and tiles are simple flat chips seated in recessed board cells with loose friction fit only (cells are for visual organization, not locking). Smallest engraved feature is the coin denomination number at approximately 6mm height, well within FDM legibility. No hardware inserts anywhere; second-lowest joint-risk item in the set after Cairn Climbers and Orbital Blockade/Meteor Field.

On the table, four square grid-boards each partially filled with small colorful square silk tiles arranged in patterns, and beside them neat stacks of round coin tokens in four graduated sizes (small copper, medium silver, larger gold, largest ornate gold) sorted by denomination. A few coins sit face-down as if mid-bid. Soft warm lighting, jewel-tone indigo-gold-teal palette, elegant overhead flat-lay product photography.

ideas.title: Kiln & Ember
ideas.concept: A set-collection game about mixing pottery glazes, where players stack translucent colored resin chips onto a lit peg board so that layering red over blue actually shows purple through the chip when held to light, and must match customer order tiles by building the exact stack composition before rivals draft the colors out from under them. Every draft decision is a bet on what color combination you can still complete.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'color mixing pigment set collection board game pottery glaze theme' and 'board game translucent stacking chips color mixing visual' — found general color-mixing games (Chroma Mix, Mix!, Color Mixing Memory) that resolve color mixing abstractly via card text or matching symbols, none using physically translucent stacked chips whose actual overlaid color is visually verifiable by the players, and none themed around pottery glaze firing. This specific physical-translucency-plus-pottery-theme combination was not found as an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: each player takes a Kiln Board (a stand with 4 vertical pegs) and 3 starting Glaze Chips of their choice from the supply bag. Shuffle 30 Order Tiles (each specifies a target peg composition by exact count and color, e.g. '1 Red + 2 Blue') into a face-up row of 4. Fill the Market Row with 6 face-up Glaze Chips drawn from the bag (colors: Red, Blue, Yellow are Primary; Purple, Green, Orange are Secondary, drawn less frequently at a fixed 4:4:4:2:2:2 ratio in the supply). On your turn, take one action: Draft (take 1 chip from the Market Row into your personal reserve, refill the row from the bag) or Stack (move any number of chips from your reserve onto one peg on your Kiln Board, in any order) or Fulfill (if one of your pegs' current chip stack exactly matches a face-up Order Tile's specified composition — same colors, same counts, order of stacking irrelevant — claim that tile, score its points immediately, remove the chips from the peg back to the box, refill the Order row). Game ends when the Order Tile deck is exhausted or any player fulfills their 5th order; highest total points wins; ties broken by most unused reserve chips.
ideas.components: 4x Kiln Boards (PLA opaque white, 100x100mm base with 4 vertical pegs 60mm tall); 60x Glaze Chips (translucent PLA/PETG, 25mm diameter x4mm thick discs with a center through-hole, approximately 18 each in translucent red/blue/yellow plus 8 each in pre-mixed translucent purple/green/orange); 30x Order Tiles (PLA, 35mm engraved discs specifying composition); 1x Chip supply canister (PLA, 100mm diameter lidded canister with a shake-and-draw slot); 1x storage box (PLA lidded box, 230x230x80mm with a peg-board nesting tray).
ideas.demand_case: Set-collection is one of BGG's most common mechanics (2,500+ tagged titles) and color-mixing/pattern games in the family-weight space have proven sustained retail demand (Qwirkle-style pattern/color games remain perennial bestsellers in the family category per major retailer bestseller lists). Target audience: family game night, ages 8+, and craft-hobbyist crossover buyers drawn to the pottery theme.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn — draft a chip you need now versus one a rival is clearly collecting toward, and when to lock a peg's stack in for a visible order versus holding for a bigger one — is the same proven drafting tension that makes set-collection games like Splendor and Ticket to Ride engaging, sharpened here by the physical, verifiable trick of actually seeing the mixed color through translucent stacked chips, which gives immediate tactile feedback that abstract color-matching games lack. 30-40 minute playtime and light-medium complexity fit the stated family audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 unique part types; the peg-and-chip stack is a simple, well-validated peg-in-hole joint (chips have a center through-hole sized ~0.5mm larger than the peg diameter for free stacking, no press-fit precision needed since chips aren't meant to lock). The only material consideration flagged for the modeler: chips must be printed in translucent PLA/PETG filament rather than opaque, which is a standard filament swap, not a geometry risk, and the color-mixing visual effect (viewing stacked translucent chips against light) is a well-understood optical property of translucent FDM prints at this thickness, not an unvalidated mechanism — the game's actual scoring rule is a simple count-and-color match, so even if a given light-viewing effect looks subtly different across print batches, it never affects the ability to play or score correctly.
